title: 2 — Controversial Coffee
paragraphs: Is Entropy Subjective?
Maria Violaris

Entropy is a central concept in many contexts such as thermodynamics and statistical mechanics, yet its interpretation remains controversial. In particular, there is a longstanding debate about whether entropy is a subjective or objective entity, and what (if any) the role of an observer and their knowledge play in defining entropy. I will present a novel interpretation of entropy through a series of thought experiments based on coffee. This continues a tradition of comments about coffee in philosophical literature on entropy, which aim to demonstrate fundamental problems with our understanding of entropy or the absurdity of some of the subjective interpretations of entropy. I will argue that entropy is subjective only in the sense that it can be affected by the knowledge (true information) of an observer. I model the observer as a part of an environment, which may or may not be sensitive to different properties of a system, affecting how we quantify the system’s entropy. In my interpretation, entropy does not depend on the subjective beliefs of the observer, avoiding many critiques of subjective entropy through common sense arguments about how our beliefs cannot affect a thermodynamic process.
Introduction

What happens when you mix milk into your coffee? This question has perennially puzzled and divided philosophers of the foundations of thermodynamics and statistical mechanics. One key aspect about the debate over coffee is whether or not the mixing of milk depends on the presence of an observer. The solution hinges on whether our interpretation of entropy is subjective or objective. Here I will argue for an interpretation of entropy that is objective in that it does not depend on the beliefs of observers, but is subjective in that it can depend on the knowledge of observers (where “knowledge” refers to true information about a system). In my interpretation, the sensitivity of the environment to the properties of a system is key, and an observer may or may not be part of that environment and contribute to this sensitivity. By viewing the environment as a measuring device, we can gain insights into how objectively or subjectively milk mixes into coffee, which in turn serves as a toy model for entropy changes more generally.

I will begin by outlining some objections to subjective entropy. Then I will present my interpretation of the subjectivity of entropy. Next I will discuss this interpretation through a series of coffeerelated thought experiments. Finally I will consider the additional aspect of how far we can manipulate systems, and the impact of this on our ideas about entropy.
Terminology
The system is the entity for which we want to quantify the entropy changes.
The environment is the surroundings of the system.
The sensitivity of the environment is its ability to respond differently depending on differences in the possible states of the system.
An observer is a person or machine with knowledge about the system, in the environment of the system.
Knowledge is true information that the observer has about the possible states of the system.
Objections to Subjective Entropy

Objections to subjective entropy have been made on a variety of grounds. For instance, Goldstein suggests that there are three key problems: prediction of wrong values, lack of explanatory and predictive power, and the fact that phase points play no role.[1] Here I will focus on the argument based on lack of explanatory power. This style of argument is generally the notion that it is absurd for entropy changes to depend on observers, since they occur autonomously and independently of observation.
Goldstein explains:

“In the absence of observers, does heat flow from the cooler to the hotter? In distant stars, does heat flow from the cooler to the hotter? In the days before humans existed, did heat flow from the cooler to the hotter? After the human race becomes extinct, will heat flow from the cooler to the hotter? If not, why would observers be relevant at all to the explanation of the phenomenon?”

These questions from Goldstein aim to demonstrate the absurdity of subjective entropy—it seems obvious that heat must flow from the cooler to the hotter, irrespective of whether there are humans there or not. The thermodynamic processes in stars must continue to occur when there are no observers, or this would make understanding thermodynamics before humanity impossible. It therefore seems compelling that there is objective entropy, described by objective laws.
Goldstein makes a similar argument about prediction:
“Can we predict that heat will flow from the hotter to the cooler in the absence of observers? If so, why would observers be relevant to the prediction?”

This emphasises the problems for the structure of science and its aim of prediction if we are constrained to only predicting the future of thermodynamic processes in the presence of observers. We would be unable to make predictions for the vast array of unobserved phenomena that should be in the domain of science.
These arguments echo those made by other philosophers in relation to applying subjective entropy to mixing milk in coffee, for instance Albert:

“Can anybody seriously think that our merely being ignorant of the exact microconditions of thermodynamic systems plays some part in bringing it about, in making it the case, that (say) milk [mixes into] coffee? How could that be? What can all those guys have been up to?”[2]

Here Albert highlights that the processes taking place when milk is mixed into coffee are independent of a human’s knowledge: the exact same process would happen whether or not the human had knowledge of it. Both of these objections therefore focus on the absurdity of our ignorance affecting the autonomous flow of thermodynamic processes.

I will argue that a human’s knowledge of the microconditions of the coffee does play a role in quantifying the entropy change as milk mixes into coffee. However, this is not to say that it affects the microphysics happening in the coffee—it only tells us how to quantify that microphysics in terms of entropy. Prompted by Goldstein and Albert’s objections, one might ask: if the microphysics is the same with and without this knowledge, then what physical difference could an associated entropy change possibly be causing? I propose that there is a physical impact from the entropy change. The catch is that, counterintuitively, this physical impact is not on the coffee in isolation. Instead, it depends on the environment of the coffee, and what properties of the coffee the environment is sensitive to. For example, if the environment is an observer, the observer with knowledge has a greater space of possible physical actions than an observer without knowledge. This view is similar to Maxwell’s view of thermodynamics as “means-relative”—dependent on the information and manipulative ability of an observer.[3]

However, the environment need not be an observer for the entropy change to have physical consequences. I will argue that characterizing entropy changes does not only rely on an _observer_ having information and manipulative ability, but more generally on _any_ animate or inanimate environment that is sensitive to changes in the properties of a system.
The Environment as a Measuring Device

Now I will outline my interpretation of entropy, which allows us to make sense of the role of an observer in quantifying the entropy changes of a system. In this view, the key determinant of the entropy changes of a system is its environment. The environment acts as a measurement device performing measurements on the system. For the interaction between the system and environment to be considered a “measurement”, distinct states of the system must cause the environment to enter distinct states. The environment therefore becomes correlated with the property of the system being measured.

Under what conditions can an environment act as a measurer? _It_ must have at least two distinguishable states, so that it can distinguish between the measured property of the _system_ having one value or another. This is similar to the conditions for a medium to be an information medium in the constructor theory of information.[4] An environment that can encode information (and hence satisfies the requirements to be an information medium) can also encode a measurement result.

A more sensitive environment will change according to more finegrained changes in properties of the system. This applies whether or not an observer is present in that environment. But let’s consider the case where an observer is there with some measurement devices. The observer’s measurement devices influence the sensitivity of the environment to the system’s state. Meanwhile, that observer’s knowledge influences what kind of measurement devices they can create. The sensitivity of the observer’s measuring device is therefore downstream from the observer’s knowledge about what kind of measurement device they can create. When we take this view, the entropy of the system is objective in the sense that it only depends on the objective sensitivity of the environment to the properties of the system. However, it is subjective in the sense that it _can_ (but does not have to) depend on observers’ knowledge about the system, since this is a factor which affects the measuring devices they can create and hence the environment’s sensitivity to the system. Even without an observer, if the environment is sensitive to the changes of a system in a particular degree of freedom—acting as a measuring device—then we can still quantify entropy changes in that degree of freedom.
Let me apply this argument to describe what happens when milk is mixed into coffee.

The system here is the coffee, which consists of water and milk that are initially separated. If there is an inanimate environment with no observer (and no specially tailored machine to distinguish milk and coffee) present, then the mixing of the milk into the coffee makes no difference to the environment.

In this scenario, it is meaningless to ask whether the milk is mixed into the coffee. There is no way in which the milk being mixed into the coffee could affect the environment unless we have some kind of measuring instrument able to distinguish between milk and water. A sceptic may see this as epitomising the problem with subjective entropy: for the milk mixes into the coffee irrespective of whether there is a measuring instrument (such as a human eye or tongue) there to detect it.

One response is that when there is no measuring instrument, there is any number of descriptions of the coffee’s evolution, and the only reason we would consider the milk mixing with the coffee is because we have natural measuring instruments sensitive to changes in how milk is mixed with coffee. For instance, it may be that some coffee molecules are heavier than others, so the composition of the coffee molecules is different at the top and bottom of the coffee cup. We would not normally be sensitive to these differences, hence we would not consider the mixing of the light and heavy coffee molecules as an entropy change in the coffee. But if we invented some glasses that made visible the difference between the light and heavy molecules, then we would conclude that there is an entropy change when the coffee is mixed.

This logic is similar to that needed to understand the Gibbs paradox. If we begin with a container with two distinguishable gases and then remove a dividing wall, the entropy of the container will increase as the gases mix. However, if the gases are identical, exactly the same micro-physics as in the “mixing” situation could happen, but there would be no entropy change.[5] As with the coffee, when we are sensitive to the difference between the gases, there is an entropy change, whereas when we are insensitive to the difference, there is no entropy change. If we were ignorant of the difference between two distinguishable gases, some might argue that we would ascribe the wrong entropy change of zero to the mixing process. By contrast, in my interpretation, the entropy change is zero, since there is no measuring instrument able to distinguish the gases.

Hence when there are no measuring instruments present, there is just as much reason to consider the milk mixing into the coffee as a significant entropy change as there is to consider ordinarily imperceptible mixing of light and heavy coffee molecules as one. Yet we would not consider the latter as significant because the environment is not sensitive to it—we have no measuring instruments that detect such a difference between the light and heavy molecules. The act of making a distinction between milk and water, to describe the process of milk mixing with water, presumes the existence of a sensitive environment, namely measuring devices able to distinguish the milk and water. With an environment insensitive to the difference between milk and water, we cannot deduce the entropy changes when you mix milk and water, because the question itself is making an assumption about the environment’s sensitivity.
Coffee with an Alien

To emphasise this point, let us consider the coffee cup of an observer that is different to humans: an alien. The alien has alien coffee mixed with alien milk. Human senses are unable to distinguish between alien milk and alien water, so if a human observer attempts to observe the mixing of alien milk with alien coffee, they will have precisely the same experience as they would have had they observed a cup of alien coffee without any milk mixed in. If an alien asks a human what happened to the alien coffee while alien milk was mixed in, they will say “nothing”. Milk only mixed into coffee for those observers able to distinguish the milk and coffee—those sensitive to the difference either directly through their senses or through some other kind of measuring instrument. The key is that the difference between milk and coffee must have some macroscopic effect on the environment. This is a requirement for any work to be extracted from the process, which is a key implication of any entropy changes. In other words, an objective quantity, the amount of extractable work, depends on the states between which the “subjective” observer is capable of distinguishing.

Now the entropy changes in the system depend on whether or not the environment is a measurer of the properties of the system that we are considering for the entropy changes. The alien is a measurer for alien tea, and humans are measurers for human tea, but they may not be measurers for each other’s tea. Therefore, the entropy changes that they each register for alien tea compared to human tea will be different.

This example demonstrates that entropy is subjective in the sense that it can depend on the observer, since different observers may have different sensitivity to changes in a system. If the humans had knowledge of how to distinguish alien milk and coffee, and vice versa, then the humans and aliens would register the same entropy changes. Therefore, entropy depends on the sensitivity of the environment, including the sensitivity of the observer, which can be increased through the observer gaining additional knowledge of how to build better (more sensitive) technology.
Thermally-Isolated Coffee

Now I will focus on a particular concern of Goldstein’s on the direction of the flow of heat. Rather than the milk mixing into the coffee, let us now consider the coffee cooling as it warms its surroundings. Goldstein suggests that subjective entropy is problematic because it implies that heat only flows from hotter to colder bodies in the presence of observers. He questions whether, in the absence of observers, heat could flow from colder to hotter bodies.

In my framework, an “observer” is just one component of the environment, and the important aspect of the environment is its sensitivity to different properties of the system’s state. Entropy changes are only well-defined when the environment has the measurement capabilities to distinguish between states of the system. An observer with knowledge about the system could construct measuring instruments sensitive to properties of the system that the naturally occurring environment would not be. There is no distinction between an observer’s measurement of a system or an environment being sensitive to the properties of a system in the sense that both are capable of measuring, and being affected by, a certain set of distinguishable states of the system. Hence if we try and apply the concerns of Goldstein to my framework, the question “In the absence of observers, does heat flow from the cooler to the hotter?” should be replaced by the question “In the absence of an environment, does heat flow from the cooler to the hotter?” My response to this question is _yes_, heat can flow from the cooler to the hotter (and vice versa) in the absence of an environment. This spontaneous heat flow does not defy any laws of thermodynamics. To explain why, I will consider the thermodynamics of a thermally-isolated cup of coffee.

Consider the process whereby the coffee cools slightly due to warming the cold cup in which it is poured, but the entire cup is somehow thermally isolated from the environment. The environment is entirely insensitive to temperature changes across the system, therefore we cannot consider the temperature changes as entropy changes. As Erik Curiel points out, “there is no such thing, not even in principle, as an entropometer”—our quantification of entropy is entirely dependent on the parameters of the system we choose to be sensitive to, and hence on the environment that is able to interact with the system. One way to see this is to consider how reversible the warming of the coffee cup is—essentially rephrasing our question to: “In the absence of an environment, could heat flow from the hotter to the cooler be reversed?”

It could be technologically possible to have a high degree of control over the particles in the coffee and coffee cup. With some combination of electromagnetic fields, we could manipulate the coffee cup such that it is in a state where coffee absorbs heat from the cup. Yet, this would not defy the second law of thermodynamics, since there is no way we could extract work from this process. Coupling the reverse-coffee cup with an environment in an attempt to extract work would disturb the system such that the apparent reverse heat flow would not become an entropy change that we can harness.

This is essentially using the warming coffee-cup (and the reverse) as a large-scale generalisation of the spin-echo experiment. In this experiment, a spin magnetic moment in a magnetic field evolves from a low coarse-grained entropy state to a high coarse-grained entropy state. We can then reverse the direction of the field, and the spin magnetic moment will evolve back from the high entropy state to the low entropy state. With a high degree of control, we can therefore reverse the apparent entropy increase.

However, while our sensitivity to the system enables us to reverse the entropy increase, note that we are unable to extract work whilst maintaining these reversible entropy changes in the system. From a coarse-grained perspective, the initial state of the spin-echo is lowentropy, and the final state is high-entropy. In principle, the initial low-entropy state could be used as fuel for an engine to extract work, leaving the system in a high-entropy state at the end. But in this case, it would be impossible to do the spin-echo style reversal of the high-entropy final state of the system back into the low-entropy initial state. This is because its interaction with the environment, specifically the work extraction system, gets rid of the detailed microstate (“fine-grained”) information that is needed to reverse it back to the low-entropy initial state. You can think of the information needed for reversal as having been transferred to the environment.
An approach to understanding the spin-echo experiment is made by Ridderbos and Redhead, where they make the following comments that I argue can also be applied in the coffee-cup example:[6]

“The only method we have of measuring the entropy of the system actually alters the state of the system. [...] It is the interaction of the spin system with its environment which enables the system to achieve a true equilibrium state. […] Since an isolated system will retain its coherence, the only way to account for non-equilibrium behavior is to focus on the fact that no physical system can be completely isolated from its environment. [...] It is the fact that thermodynamic systems are limited, nonisolated systems which gives rise to the emergence of irreversible behaviour.”

The core of their argument is that a system can _appear_ to evolve from a state of low-entropy to high-entropy by some coarse-grained definition of entropy. However, providing the system is isolated, all the information about the initial state is contained in correlations between different parts of the system. Unless the information in these correlations is ignored (e.g., by coarse-graining) or the correlations are destroyed (e.g., by interaction with an environment), then the evolution of the system is, in principle, reversible. Hence the finegrained entropy of an isolated system cannot have changed. This ultimately can be applied to the universe as a whole: “Since the universe itself does not have an environment to interact with, it follows that its entropy must be constant in time.”

This may come as a surprise when considering the conventional narrative surrounding the second law of thermodynamics applied to the universe: since the disorder of an isolated system is exceedingly unlikely to decrease, the universe as a whole is tending towards disorder and ultimately a heat death. However, this can only be the case if microstate information is getting lost somewhere; and if the universe is truly isolated, then at the most fine-grained scale possible, its entropy cannot change and must remain constant. It neither increases nor decreases in a violation of the second law.

In the view I am elaborating, any system—whether the spin-echo experiment, a warming coffee cup, or any type of heat dissipation—only has a change in fine-grained entropy if it interacts with an environment. I extend this statement to say that the environment is a necessary but insufficient requirement for an entropy change in a system. It is almost always sufficient for entropy change due to heat dissipation. For more obscure scenarios such as the interaction of gases of different chemical isotopes, a more specialised environment (possibly a measuring instrument created by a knowledgeable observer) is necessary for there to be an entropy change.

Returning to Goldstein’s objections to subjective entropy on the grounds of absurdity: why is it that heat flow appears to be so objective and autonomous—can it really depend on the sensitivity of an environment of a system in which heat flow is taking place, rather than an inherent property of the system with heat flowing? The possibility of reverse heat-flow in an isolated system appears counterintuitive because it is rare for the environment to be thermally isolated from a system. Normally, all systems have some thermal contact with their surroundings, so the environment is sensitive to changes in temperature. The cooling coffee is an example where the environment is always sensitive to heat and therefore we always see the system being “measured”, causing the subjective entropy sceptics to question what role the observer can have. The solution is that the environment is automatically a measurer of heat differences because of the thermal contact between system and environment.

By contrast, in other scenarios the system can have properties that a typical environment is very insensitive to. For instance, a typical environment may not be able to distinguish between chemical isotopes of a system. These cases are the ones where detailed knowledge from an observer becomes important, because such an observer could intelligently build a measuring instrument capable of distinguishing the changes in the relevant property of the system. In such a scenario, it is much more intuitive to see the need for an environment, and even for an observer, in order to quantify the entropy changes.
Multi-Coloured Microstate Coffee

I will now consider a thought experiment to emphasise the notion that an observer could intelligently build a detection instrument to vastly increase the sensitivity of the environment to the system. Once again, the system is a cup of coffee.

The most extreme way of distinguishing between the different properties of a cup of coffee would be if we could distinguish between the microstates of the coffee. Imagine if we built an instrument that was sensitive to the microstate of the coffee. For example, it could be an imaging device which scans the coffee cup and outputs the position of all the individual molecules to some precision. Each possible combination of molecule positions could be assigned a number on a scale from 0 to 1. Then that number could be used to correspond to some colour on the spectrum of visible light from blue to red. Then a machine could modify the colour of the coffee cup according to the coffee’s microstate. As someone stirs their coffee, they can see the colour of the coffee cup changing according to its microstate (coarse-grained to some finite precision, but this can be done to arbitrary accuracy for arbitrarily small fine-graining). With this colour-changing coffee cup, we may interpret the mixing of milk into coffee differently. Now each of the unmixed and mixed microstates has different macroscopic properties. So essentially as you mix the milk, the coffee microstates remain just as distinguishable—the only thing you see is the coffee moving through different colours.

Each microstate of the mixed coffee is just as distinct and unique as any other. If you could not distinguish the mixed microstates, it would look like entropy has increased as the coffee is mixed, because each mixed microstate is only one out of a large set of possible mixed microstates. But now each of these microstates is distinguishable, the coffee is just tracing through each of them, and they are not part of a larger set of indistinguishable states. The entropy of the coffee remains constant.
The Coffee Machine

So far, I have been focusing on the sensitivity of the environment to the states of the system. However we are often interested in the entropy changes of a system for operational reasons—for instance, we would like to know whether or not we can reverse the evolution that occurred. Being able to track the fine-grained microstate of the system does not imply that we are able to control that microstate and reverse the evolution. High sensitivity of the environment is a necessary but not sufficient condition to be able to additionally manipulate the system.

Just how much we can manipulate the system depends on which entity does the manipulation. To avoid any trivial manipulation being possible with enough resources, we can impose the condition that the entity should be able to manipulate the system in a cycle for its manipulations to be possible. Within this framework, a manipulation of a system being possible does not imply that the reverse manipulation is possible. Therefore there is a potential irreversibility that emerges with respect to what one can and cannot do to a system. In the constructor theory of thermodynamics, this is conjectured to be the true source of _exact_ irreversibility in thermodynamics, as opposed to approximative, statistical explanations of the second law.[7]

Returning to the example of coffee, let us consider how far we could manipulate a coffee cup to mix together the milk with the coffee, and to unmix them. They could be mixed with a relatively simple machine: a spoon. The spoon can operate in a cycle, so the mixing is a possible manipulation. However, there is no simple entity that can perform the reverse process of unmixing the milk and coffee in a cycle (without side-effects). Hence the observer-dependent view of entropy presented here is consistent with irreversibility emerging on the level of what we can and cannot do to our coffee, even though the fully fine-grained entropy of the coffee would remain constant with complete information about its microstate.
Conclusion

Entropy is notoriously difficult to characterise. There is a multitude of definitions of entropy spanning a range of contexts, from the multiple definitions of entropy in statistical mechanics to information and quantum information theory. There is a longstanding debate about whether entropy is an entity that exists objectively in the universe, in a similar way to energy, or whether entropy is a subjective or anthropomorphic concept. Here I have argued that entropy is both objective and subjective, in the sense that it does not depend on the beliefs of an observer, but it does depend on the sensitivity of the environment, which can vary depending on the knowledge of an observer controlling the environment. I have illustrated this suggestion through a series of thought experiments centred around the classic example of mixing milk into coffee.
